title: Expository Commentary on the Sutra of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha
excerpt: The Indian Tripitaka Master Kang Sengkai translated this sutra during the Cao Wei dynasty.

inline.s: The Indian Tripitaka Master Kang Sengkai translated this sutra during the Cao Wei dynasty.
The commentary was composed by the monk Huiyuan of Jingying Temple in the capital city, during the Sui dynasty.

blocks.text: Expository Commentary on the Sutra of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha, Fascicle One

inline.s: [Commentary]

The sacred teachings are not all alike; in brief there are just two. The first is the Sravaka Pitaka, the second the Bodhisattva Pitaka. Teaching the Dharma for sravakas is called the Sravaka Pitaka; teaching the Dharma for bodhisattvas is called the Bodhisattva Pitaka. Within the Sravaka Pitaka what is taught is twofold: first sravakas who are sravakas, second pratyekabuddhas who are sravakas. The sravakas who are sravakas are persons who in the past sought the path of the sravaka, constantly delighting in contemplating the four Noble Truths, and so formed the nature of a sravaka; in their last body they met the Buddha, who spoke the Dharma of the four Truths for them, and they awakened to the Way. Their original nature was that of a sravaka, and now again hearing the voice they awakened to the Way; therefore they are called sravakas who are sravakas. The sutra says, 'For those who seek to be sravakas he spoke the Dharma of the four Truths'; this is what is meant. The pratyekabuddhas who are sravakas are persons who originally sought the path of the pratyekabuddha, constantly delighting in contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, and so formed the nature of a pratyekabuddha; in their last body they met the Buddha, who spoke the Dharma of the twelve links for them, and they awakened to the Way. Their original nature was that of a pratyekabuddha, and in their last body they heard the voice and awakened to the Way; therefore they are called pratyekabuddhas who are sravakas. The sutra says, 'For those who seek pratyekabuddhahood he spoke the twelve links.' On this basis, though the two attainments differ, they both receive the Lesser Dharma and both in the present life hear the voice and awaken to the Way; therefore what is spoken to these two kinds of persons is the Sravaka Pitaka. Within the Bodhisattva Pitaka there are two divisions: first the gradual, second the sudden. As to the gradual entrant, he is a person who in the past studied the Great Dharma, in the meantime practiced the Lesser and realized the Lesser fruit, and later returned to the Great, coming from the Lesser; this is called gradual. Therefore the sutra says, 'Except those who formerly practiced and studied the Lesser Vehicle, I shall also cause them to enter this Dharma'; this is the gradual entrance. As to sudden awakening, there are sentient beings who for a long time have cultivated the good roots corresponding to the Great Vehicle; now for the first time seeing the Buddha they are able to enter the Great. The Great does not come from the Lesser; because of this it is called sudden. Therefore the sutra says, 'Or there are sentient beings who age after age have always received my teaching; when first they see my body and hear what I say they all at once believe and receive, entering the wisdom of the Tathagata'; this is sudden awakening. The gradual-entering bodhisattva relies on shallow stages and journeys far; the suddenly-awakening bodhisattva in a single leap understands the Great. Though sudden and gradual differ, since they then both receive the Great in one place, therefore what is spoken to these two kinds of persons is the Bodhisattva Pitaka. Though the sacred teachings are many, they do not go beyond these two. Therefore Nagarjuna said, 'After the Buddha's nirvana, Kasyapa and Ananda at Rajagrha compiled the Dharma-storehouse as the Sravaka Pitaka; Manjusri and Ananda on the Iron-Circumference Mountain compiled the Mahayana as the Bodhisattva Pitaka.' The Bodhisattva-bhumi also says, 'The Buddha spoke the sutras for those sravakas and bodhisattvas practicing the way that escapes suffering; the compilers gathered them into two Pitakas; for speaking what the sravakas practice is the Sravaka Pitaka, and speaking what the bodhisattvas practice is the Bodhisattva Pitaka.' Therefore we know the sacred teachings do not go beyond these two. These two are also called the Great Vehicle and the Lesser Vehicle, the complete and the incomplete teachings; though the names are inverted and changed, their meaning is not different. Now this sutra, within the two Pitakas, is gathered into the Bodhisattva Pitaka; it is the Dharma-wheel of sudden teaching for those of sharp and ripened faculties. How do we know it is sudden? This sutra is precisely for those among ordinary people who dread birth and death and seek right concentration, causing them to rouse the mind to be born in the Pure Land; it does not proceed from the Lesser or the Great; therefore we know it is sudden.
[Commentary]

Having distinguished the divisions, next we explain the title. Now 'the Sutra of Immeasurable Life spoken by the Buddha' sets forth the separate name of the sutra. All the sutras put the title first to show the Dharma they set forth; this sutra reveals the practice and the attainment of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and the beings he gathers and transforms, and therefore first raises that name. But those various sutras receive their names differently: some are named only from the Dharma, as with the Nirvana and the like; some only from a person, as with the Trapusa sutra and the Prince sutra; some only from an event, as with the Withered Tree sutra; some only from a simile, as with the Great Cloud sutra and the Jewelled Casket sutra; some from the time, as with the sutra on right and wrong times; some from a place, as with the Samgha sutra and the sutra of Gaya's Peak; some raise both person and Dharma, as with the Vimalakirti sutra and the Srimati sutra; some set forth both event and Dharma, as with the Vaipulya Great Assembly sutra; some reveal both Dharma and simile, as with the Avatamsaka and the Lotus sutras; some raise both person and Dharma, as with the sutra where Sariputra asks about illness, and so forth. Thus they are not of one pattern. Now this sutra is named from the person. When first listing the person there are in all four kinds: first raising the person himself, as in the Vimalakirti and the like; second raising the asker, as in Manjusri's questions; third raising the person spoken of, as in the Prince sutra; fourth raising the person to be transformed, as in the sutra of Sumati's daughter and the Jade sutra. Now the opening of this sutra generally raises both the speaker and the one spoken of. When it first says 'the Buddha,' it raises the speaker; 'Immeasurable Life' raises the spoken of. The occasions of preaching differ, five in all, as Nagarjuna says: first the Buddha speaks himself; second holy worthies speak; third the gods speak; fourth gods and immortals speak; fifth transformed persons speak. This sutra is spoken by the Buddha, and to set it apart from the other four the word 'Buddha' is raised. 'Buddha' is a foreign word translated as 'the awakened.' 'Awakened' has two senses. First, awareness, directed at the affliction-obstacle; affliction harms, its affair being like a thief, and only sages are aware of it and are not harmed by it; therefore it is called 'awakened.' This sense is explained as in the Nirvana. Second, comprehension, directed at the wisdom-obstacle; ignorance lies sleeping, its affair being like sleep, and when sage-wisdom arises one awakens greatly, as one wakes from sleep; therefore it is called 'awakened.' The ignorance that is its object is of two kinds: first, the nature-veiling ignorance, which obscures the real nature; removing it, the false turns to the true, and to awaken to the real is called 'awakened.' Second, the unknowing within events, deluded about the characteristics of dharmas; removing it, one understands all wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral dharmas, the three categories and so forth; therefore it is called 'awakened.' Therefore the Bodhisattva-bhumi says, 'In the category of benefit-to-meaning, the category of non-benefit-to-meaning, and the category of neither-benefit-nor-non-benefit, he opens and awakens equally; therefore he is called Buddha.' Benefit-to-meaning is good, non-benefit is not good, neither is neutral; in all this he is fully aware; therefore he is called 'awakened.' Since he awakens himself and also awakens others, and the practice of awakening is fully carried out, he is called Buddha. The self-awakening sets him apart from ordinary beings; leading on to awakening others sets him apart from the two vehicles; the practice of awakening fully complete sets him apart from bodhisattvas; therefore only he alone is called Buddha. Uttering with the mouth is called 'speaking.' 'Immeasurable Life' is what is spoken. This sutra proclaims the practice and the attainment of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the beings he gathers and transforms. As to 'practice,' it proclaims the vows he first made and the practice he first cultivated. As to 'attainment,' it speaks of the two fruits he now attains, the Dharma-body and the Pure Land. As to 'gathering,' he universally gathers the connected sentient beings of the ten directions so that they all go together to that land; the benefit of the Dharma-transformation is called 'the gathered.' Moreover, all the bodhisattvas now study his practice, obtain his attainment, and share his gathering; this is called 'the gathered.' These distinctions cannot be fully enumerated; since the virtues are gathered from the person, therefore it is simply said to speak of Immeasurable Life. The Buddha's name is of two kinds, the common and the particular. 'Thus-come One, Worthy of Offerings' and the like are the common names; 'Sakyamuni, Maitreya, Immeasurable Life' and the like are the particular designations. In the particular names established there are many kinds: some from the lineage, as Sakyamuni Buddha, Kasyapa Buddha, and so forth; some from the body, as the Honored Body Buddha and the Body Above Buddha; some from the voice, as the Wonderful Sound Buddha and the Fine Voice Buddha; some from the light, as the Universal Light Buddha; some from inner virtue, some based on a simile; thus they are not one. This Buddha is named from his lifespan. The lifespan has a true and an apparent one; the true is eternally abiding, its nature the same as empty space; the apparent lifespan is not fixed, sometimes long, sometimes short. What is discussed here is the apparent, not the true. Within the apparent lifespan this Buddha's life is long, and ordinary beings and the two vehicles cannot fathom its limit; therefore it is called 'immeasurable.' The life-span is called 'lifespan.' How do we know it is apparent and not true? As the Sutra of Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta says, though the lifespan of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is long and far-reaching, it too has an end; after that Buddha's nirvana, Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta in succession become Buddhas; therefore we know it is apparent. 'Sutra' is the foreign word 'sutra,' translated as 'thread.' The sayings of sages can string all dharmas, as a thread strings flowers; therefore it is called 'thread.' And saying 'sutra,' the thread can string flowers and the sutra can maintain the lifespan; their function being similar, therefore it is called 'sutra.' If one follows the ordinary gloss, 'sutra' means 'constant.' People differ in past and present, but the teachings are an enduring norm; therefore it is called 'constant.' How are 'sutra' and 'constant' related? Interpreting 'sutra' by 'constant,' the explanation is that 'sutra' means to pass through; any one Dharma passes through antiquity and reaches the present, always existing without interruption; this is its sense of 'constant'; therefore it is called 'constant.'

From beginning to end this sutra's text has no more than three [divisions]: the preface, the main teaching, and the transmission. From the beginning to 'he replied, 'I wish to hear them'' is its preface. From 'The Buddha told Ananda, 'In the past, long ago...'' onward is the main teaching. From 'The Buddha told Maitreya, 'Those who shall hear that Buddha's name and rejoice''' onward is the transmission. Transformation must have a cause, so the preface is first shown. Since the preface has arisen, the main doctrine is next set forth; therefore second the main teaching is distinguished. The sages preach the Dharma for the benefit of the various beings; having finished preaching the sutra, they praise its excellence, urge study, and entrust it for preservation; therefore third the transmission is distinguished.
[Commentary]

Within the preface the meaning and text, though many, have an essential meaning of only two: first the initiating preface, second the attesting-faith preface. When the Buddha is about to teach the sutra, he first relies on the time and place, uses supernatural power to gather the assembly, and raises the principle of what is taught; this is called 'initiating.' As it is the cause of the teaching, it is called the initiating preface. As to the attesting-faith preface, after the Buddha has finished teaching the sutra, Ananda receives it and, about to transmit it to later ages, first says to the assembly, 'Such is the Dharma, I heard it from the Buddha,' attesting it so as to be credible; this is called 'attesting faith.' Because this attestation is the cause of transmitting the sutra, it is called the attesting-faith preface. For what reason are these two prefaces established? First, because there are two sutras. The sutra is only one; how has there ever been two? Though the substance of the sutra is one, measured by persons and times it is divided in two: first the sutra spoken by the Tathagata, second the sutra transmitted by Ananda. The Tathagata's speech benefited that time; Ananda's transmission is transmitted to later ages. Facing these two sutras, therefore two prefaces are established: facing the Tathagata's sutra the initiating preface is established, and facing Ananda's transmitted sutra the attesting-faith preface is established. Moreover these two prefaces have many more meanings, all as set forth in the usual explanations.

In the text the first words, 'Thus have I heard,' are the attesting-faith preface. From 'at one time' onward the meaning has two aspects. If one takes the meaning of the original event's arising, it is assigned to the initiating [preface]; and Ananda cites it to attest the truth and make it credible, [so] it is called the attesting-faith [preface]. Since the meaning has both aspects, one cannot take it one-sidedly.
I have heard thus.

In the attesting-faith preface there are three gates of division: first, explaining the reason for the words 'Thus have I heard'; second, clarifying the purpose of establishing them; third, explaining their text.
[Commentary]

As to the reason for them, why is it that every sutra's opening has the words 'Thus have I heard'? It is because the Buddha directed [that they be] placed. Why did the Buddha direct this? Because of Ananda's request. Why did he request? Because Aniruddha instructed him. Why did Aniruddha instruct? Because he saw Ananda's mind grieved and distressed. Why was the monk Ananda grieved? Because he saw the Tathagata about to enter parinirvana. The Buddha was about to pass away, lying with his head to the north between the twin sala trees; at that time Ananda, seeing the Buddha about to end, wept and sobbed and could not contain himself. Aniruddha awakened Ananda, saying, 'You are the transmitter of the Dharma; why do you not ask the Buddha about the affairs of the future world? Of what use is mere grief?' Ananda replied, 'My mind has sunk in a sea of sorrow; what is there even to ask?' Aniruddha thereupon taught Ananda to ask four matters: first, asking that after the World-Honored One's nirvana the monks rely on what as teacher; second, asking that after the World-Honored One's nirvana the monks abide by what; third, asking how to dwell with ill-natured monks; fourth, asking what word should be set at the head of all sutras. Being instructed, Ananda's mind was somewhat awakened, and he accordingly asked the Buddha, and the Buddha answered as follows. 'The monks relying on what as teacher' means they should rely on the Pratimoksa as teacher; if I were still in the world it would be no different from this. The Pratimoksa is the precepts, what the monks study; therefore it is called their teacher. 'Monks abiding by what' means they should abide by the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four foundations of mindfulness? The monk relies on the inner body to cultivate contemplation of the body, striving with diligence to remove worldly craving and love; likewise with the outer body and the inner-outer body, and likewise with feelings, mind, and dharmas. This is called the monks' abiding place. Therefore the sutra says, 'If one abides in the four foundations of mindfulness, this is called one's own realm, and one is not bound by Mara; if one abides in the five desires, that is called Mara's realm and one is bound by Mara.' 'How to dwell with ill-natured monks' means to govern them with the brahma-danda (the penalty of silence); the brahma-danda is to be silent and not speak with them; if the mind is tamed, then one speaks of leaving the two extremes. 'What word should be set at the head of all sutras' means one should set 'Thus have I heard, the Buddha dwelt in such a place,' among such an assembly, and the other six matters. Because the Buddha thus directed, every sutra's opening is furnished with 'Thus have I heard.' This first gate being finished, next the purpose of establishing them is distinguished. What was the Buddha's intent in directing this phrase to be set? It was to produce faith in beings. 'Thus' — how does this produce faith? As to 'thus,' Ananda sets forth that he himself believed and obeyed the Buddha's words: he says the Buddha's speech was 'thus' and says what the Buddha said was 'so,' causing other beings to join him in producing faith. As to 'I have heard' — if it were to produce faith, Ananda is himself an insufficient person; if he said this Dharma was his own teaching, many would despise and slander it; because he says this Dharma was heard from the Buddha, people all turn to faith. What meaning is there in faith, that one must set up this phrase to produce it? The explanation is that faith is the first gate of entering the Dharma and the foremost in embracing the Dharma; whoever enters the Buddha-Dharma must first produce faith. Therefore the Avatamsaka says faith is the hand: as a man with a hand, on reaching a place of treasures, takes whatever he wishes; a man without hands obtains nothing. So too whoever enters the Buddha-Dharma, having the hand of faith, takes at will the treasure of the Way; if without faith, he gains nothing. Faith has this meaning, therefore the words 'Thus have I heard' are set up to produce faith in beings. The purpose being thus, these two gates are finished. Next the phrase 'Thus have I heard' is explained. As to 'thus,' there are two senses. First, explained by the Dharma: Ananda says the words the Buddha spoke are 'thus' with respect to dharmas, therefore called 'thus' — speaking principle as principle, events as events, cause as cause, fruit as fruit; whatever is discussed is all as the things are, therefore called 'thus.' Words that accord with the Dharma are correct in principle, therefore called 'so.' Truly, to be contrary to the Dharma is called 'not so'; therefore words that accord with the Dharma are called 'so.' Second, explained by the person: Ananda says what the present Sakyamuni spoke is 'thus' like all the Buddhas of the past; therefore called 'thus.' Therefore the Nirvana sutra says, 'As the past Buddhas spoke, not changing, therefore called

' To be contrary to the Buddhas' speech, the words are not-so; to accord with the Buddhas' speech, the words are so; therefore it is said 'thus.' As to 'I have heard,' Ananda, facing the future beings, sets forth that he himself received the teaching, therefore he says 'I have heard.' Hearing is truly with the ear; how can one say 'I'? The faculties differ, [but] all are my instruments; since it is the speaker who is set forth, therefore one says 'I have heard.' In the Dharma there is no person; where then is there an 'I'? And [yet] one speaks, based on the subject, saying 'I have heard.' The explanation is that though the Dharma has no fixed subject, it is not without a provisional name that governs, and one may also say 'I.' Therefore the Nirvana says, as four armies combined form an army, though there is no fixed commander, one may still say 'my army is valiant' and 'my army has defeated them'; this is likewise. One may ask, 'Ananda is a sage who has gained the principle; for what reason does he, like ordinary beings, say

? The explanation is that though Ananda says 'I,' he is not the same as ordinary beings. How are they different? There are three [kinds of] 'I.' First, 'I' of the view-mind: the ordinary beings have not yet lost the view of self, and in a mind of self-view they say 'there is an I.' Second, 'I' of the pride-mind: the trainees, though the view of self is gone, still have pride; in a mind of pride they say 'I.' Third, 'I' of worldly convention: the sages beyond training, whose view-impurities have long been gone and whose pride-impurity is also exhausted, follow the worldly convention and provisionally say 'I.' Now Ananda, when compiling the Dharma, was in the stage beyond training, his views and pride removed; following worldly convention he provisionally said 'I'; therefore he is not the same as ordinary beings. One may ask, '
is a provisional name of worldly truth; the no-self is the supreme truth. Why not take the supreme, and proclaim no-self, rather than follow the provisional name of worldly truth to say

?' Because the transformation of ordinary beings requires it thus: if one did not say 'I,' how could one distinguish this from that, and cause people to know and recognize? Therefore one must say 'I.' Hence even the Buddhas, when transforming, often say 'I,' and the wise do not find it strange.

From 'at one time' onward, though the meaning has both aspects, facing the foregoing, which is entirely the attesting-faith preface, from here on it is explained specifically as the initiating. Within it there are three: first, clarifying the Buddha as the transforming master; second, from 'with a great assembly of monks' onward, distinguishing his retinue; third, from 'at that time the World-Honored One's faculties were serene' onward, the Tathagata manifests transformation as the initiation, and Ananda makes the request.
At one time the Buddha was dwelling at Rajagrha, on Mount Grdhrakuta (Vulture Peak).
[Commentary]

In the foregoing, 'at one time' raises the Buddha's time of transformation. Saying 'the Buddha' raises the Buddha as the transforming person. 'Dwelling at Rajagrha' and the like raises the Buddha's place of transformation. As to 'at one time,' people have various explanations; what is set down here is this. The season of transformation is called the time. Through the Buddha's whole lifetime the times of transformation are many, and 'one' distinguishes it from the other times; therefore it is said 'one time.' The words 'at one time' abound in the sutras. As the Nirvana says, 'I, at one time, was at Rajagrha discussing worldly truth with the bodhisattva Maitreya'; 'I at one time was on the bank of the Ganges'; 'I at one time was in the cemetery of corpses.' This phrase is like those. 'The Buddha' is as explained before. 'Dwelling at Rajagrha' is a general raising by the city; in ancient times this city had many kings dwelling there, hence called Rajagrha (King's City). Mount Grdhrakuta is pointed out separately according to place; surrounding Rajagrha there are five mountains, each with a monastery; to distinguish it from the others therefore one must say Grdhrakuta. This is translated as 'Vulture Peak.' Many spirit-immortals dwell on this mountain, hence called 'spirit'; there are also vultures that roost on this mountain, hence called 'vulture'; it is also called 'Vulture-Head Mountain,' since many spirit-vultures dwell on its summit, and again the peak resembles a vulture's head. Within the place of roaming transformation, abiding is called 'dwelling.' The Dharma-body is equal and truly has no resting place, but the transformation is manifested in a direction [of space]; therefore it is said 'dwelling.' Why not take the real rather than entrust itself to transformation? In order to make the transforming teaching universal, therefore it must follow the transformation.
[Commentary]

In the second [part], the assembly, first the sravakas are listed, then the bodhisattvas are revealed. So the many sutras do; why is this? The explanation in general has four. First, distinguished by near and far: the sravakas are mostly near the Tathagata, therefore after the Buddha is clarified they are listed first as near; the bodhisattvas are mostly not near the Buddha, therefore they are listed later. Why are the sravakas especially near the Tathagata while the bodhisattvas are not? There are two senses: first, the sravakas have not practiced the Way long and are not yet familiar with the Dharma of the Way; though they have attained the sage-fruit, in their progress and deportment they always follow the Buddha's teaching, as in the vinaya it is laid down that Aniruddha should not share lodging with women, that Svagata should not drink liquor, that the seventeen youths should not play in the water, and so forth — all these are arhats following the Buddha's rules, even to the Tathagata's nirvana prescribing that the sravakas not finish the food; for this reason they are near the Buddha. The bodhisattvas, having long been familiar with the Dharma of the Way, do not rely on the Buddha's teaching, therefore they are not near the Buddha. Second, the sravakas are in this life saved by the Buddha, leaving the ordinary to become sages; the grace received being deep and heavy, though they attain the sage-fruit they always attend the Tathagata, surrounding and serving him, therefore they are mostly near the Buddha. The bodhisattvas, though they receive the Buddha's grace, in the work of transforming beings, following conditions in gathering and transforming, are mostly not near the Buddha. Because the sravakas are mostly near the Tathagata they are listed first; the bodhisattvas are not so, therefore listed later. This is the first distinction of near and far. Second, distinguished by deportment and form: the sravakas and the rest maintain their deportment, and their form resembles the Buddha, so that the world together reveres them; therefore they are listed first. The bodhisattvas, transforming according to circumstances, have indeterminate form and deportment; therefore they are listed later, as when Manjusri in a single summer dwelt in three places in retreat; this is the case. Third, distinguished by the teaching: it may also be called the distinction by the teachings. As Nagarjuna explains, the teaching has two kinds: the manifest and the secret. According to the manifest teaching, the arhats and pratyekabuddhas, like the Buddha, have the outflows extinguished, so after raising the Buddha the sravakas are first listed. The bodhisattvas, following transformation, manifest the various outflows and appear as ordinary beings; if people heard that they were above the arhats they would be much startled and surprised, therefore they are listed later. The sutras' listing the sravakas first is for the most part based on this. If one follows the profound secret teaching, the bodhisattvas' virtue is venerable and they should be first, while the sravakas' virtue is inferior and they should be later. Therefore the Avatamsaka lists the bodhisattvas first, and only later, in the assembly of the Jetavana Double-Gallery, does it list the sravakas. Fourth, distinguished by greater and lesser in number: as the Nirvana says, in any assembly the fewer are listed first and the greater later. In that sutra the sravaka assembly is small, therefore listed first, and the bodhisattva assembly is great, therefore listed later. This last sense is confined to the Nirvana; the others are common to all the sutras. Now here, relying on the first two senses, the sravakas are first listed, and then the bodhisattvas are revealed.
Within the sravaka assembly the text has four divisions: first, marking the distinction of the assembly; second, distinguishing its number; third, praising its virtue; fourth, listing its names.
Together with a great assembly of monks.
[Commentary]

First this marks the assembly; and it is by reference to the Buddha that its assembly is made clear. Taking the body together with those others is called 'together.' 'Great' is the foreign word 'maha,' translated with three senses: first called 'many,' as many people in the world are called a great assembly; second called 'surpassing,' surpassing the other practitioners, for among those ninety-five kinds of paths this is most superior, hence 'maha'; third called 'great,' broadly possessing elevated virtue, exceeding the recent learners, hence 'great.' 'Bhiksu' is a barbarian [Indian] word, translated with five senses: first 'one who frightens Mara' — at first leaving home, his roused mind is vast, causing Mara to be afraid; hence 'frightening Mara.' As the Nirvana says, why is Mara afraid? Mara's nature is jealous and mean, begrudging others surpassing himself; seeing them surpass him, he therefore harbors fear; also he fears that such a person will transform many beings and lead them all out of birth and death, emptying his realm; therefore he produces fear. This sense establishes the name from the beginning. Second, 'alms-seeker': having left home, he stores up nothing and lives by begging; hence 'alms-seeker.' Third, 'pure livelihood': in his begging he seeks alms by a right livelihood, apart from wrong livelihood; hence 'pure livelihood.' These two senses establish the name from the middle. Fourth, 'one who purely observes the precepts': having left home, he keeps the precepts purely, with no transgression; hence 'one who purely observes the precepts.' Fifth, 'one who destroys evil': because he observes the precepts he leaves the fault of transgression; hence 'destroying evil.' These last two establish the name from the end. When there are many people it is called an assembly.
Twelve thousand people were gathered together.
[Commentary]
Second, distinguishing their number. Gathering together is called 'together.'
All the great sages, whose supernormal powers have already been attained.
[Commentary]

Third, praising their virtue. 'All the great sages' praises the eminence of the persons; raising one implies the rest, hence 'all.' Those whom the dull-rooted and recent learners cannot surpass are called 'great.' 'Great' has two senses: first, high in stage and called great, as those listed below, from Ajnata Kaundinya and the rest, are all ultimate sages beyond training, surpassing the recent learners, hence called great; second, virtuous and victorious and called great, for they are all sharp-rooted sravakas accomplishing surpassing virtue, hence called great. Meeting the right is called 'sage.' 'Supernormal powers already attained' praises the excellence of their virtue; what is done is spirit-wondrous, hence called 'spirit'; without obstruction is called 'through.' 'Through' (supernormal) is of six kinds in particular: the bodily superpower, the heavenly eye, the heavenly ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the extinction of outflows; fully as in the separate chapters, and it should be fully treated here. These monks in the Lesser Vehicle have cultivated to the ultimate, hence 'already attained.' One may ask, 'Ananda, while the Buddha was alive, was in the stage of study and had not attained the extinction of outflows; how can he be named among

?' The explanation is that though Ananda was in the stage of study and not yet styled a great sage with supernormal powers attained, following the many he is praised, hence it is said 'all the great sages whose supernormal powers have already been attained.' One may ask, 'Ananda's virtue was indeed not yet complete; why is he listed in this assembly?' The explanation is that Ananda is the requester in this assembly and must be listed; moreover Ananda was of highest sharp faculties, and though in the stage of study, accomplished immeasurable sublime virtues, hence called 'great sage'; in the superpowers he comprehended ultimately, and also is called 'already attained.' Above is the praise of their virtue.

Their names are: the Venerable Ajnata Kaundinya, the Venerable Proper Vow, the Venerable Proper Speech, the Venerable Great Call, the Venerable Benevolent and Wise, the Venerable Free from Defilement, the Venerable Renowned, the Venerable Good and Real, the Venerable Complete, the Venerable Bull King, the Venerable Uruvilva Kasyapa, the Venerable Gaya Kasyapa, the Venerable Nadi Kasyapa, the Venerable Mahakasyapa, the Venerable Sariputra, the Venerable Mahamaudgalyayana, the Venerable Kapphina, the Venerable Great Abiding, the Venerable Great Pure Will, the Venerable Maha Juna, the Venerable Full of Vows, the Venerable Free from Obstacles, the Venerable Conduit, the Venerable Firm and Subduing, the Venerable Face King, the Venerable Fruit Vehicle, the Venerable Benevolent Nature, the Venerable Joy and Bliss, the Venerable Good Coming, the Venerable Rahula, the Venerable Ananda. All such as these are the elders at the head.
[Commentary]

Fourth, listing their names. Within it, first saying 'their names are' is the compiler's general raising, and next the individual listing. These all have virtue and are venerable, hence 'Venerable.' Ajnata Kaundinya: Kaundinya is the surname; Ajnata is the given, 'A' meaning 'no' and 'jna' meaning 'wisdom,' having realized the 'no' and accomplished wisdom, hence called 'no-wisdom.' 'No' is the original nature of all dharmas, called 'the original limit (bhuti)'; in this original limit he knows and sees clearly, hence 'Ajnata (knowing the original limit).' The others, some in the sutra are known and some not. Of those twelve thousand people, here just thirty-two are listed, and 'all such as these are the elders at the head' concludes the praise generally.

Next are listed the assemblies of bodhisattvas. Within it there are four: first, marking the distinction of the assembly; second, from 'Samantabhadra and the rest' listing their names; third, from 'possessing immeasurable virtues and practices' onward praising their virtue; fourth, from 'such as these, beyond recounting' onward distinguishing the total number.
Together again with the great assembly of bodhisattvas of the Great Vehicle.
[Commentary]

In the first part, 'again' is a word of repetition. Above the sravakas were listed; now the bodhisattvas are further made clear, hence 'again.' 'Together' has the same sense as before: distinguishing the Buddha and including those others, hence 'together.' As to 'Great Vehicle,' it names the Dharma to distinguish the persons. 'Vehicle' is the function of practice; practice can convey and reach, hence 'vehicle.' The vehicles are three in particular; distinguishing the other two, and the other two are not its equal, therefore it is called the Great Vehicle. 'An assembly of bodhisattvas' names the persons by the Dharma; not one is called 'assembly.' 'Bodhisattva' is a barbarian word; fully it is 'bodhisattva' (bodhi-sattva), which the transmitter abbreviated and said 'bodhisattva.' Translated here it is 'a being of the Way.' 'Bodhi' means the Way and 'sattva' means a being. For this person inwardly seeks the Way and fully possesses the practice of the Way, and is completed by the Way; hence he is called a being of the Way. One may ask, 'The sravakas and the pratyekabuddhas also all seek the Way, and all have the practice of the Way, and are all completed by the same Way; why is only this one called a being of the Way?' The explanation is that the worthy and the sages have names that are both common and particular. Common to them, the meaning is universal, as the Nirvana says — for that text says the stream-enterer and the rest are also called bodhisattva, because they seek the wisdom of the extinction of outflows and the knowledge of no-birth; they are also called Buddha, because of the common and not-common right enlightenment. But now, in order to distinguish the worthy and the sages, therefore the beings of the Great Vehicle are specifically named 'bodhisattva.' Why is only the Great Vehicle being named 'bodhisattva' among the worthy and sages? There are three senses. First, distinguished by the vow-mind looking toward the fruit: only these beings seek the great bodhi; the others do not seek it; therefore only these are called beings of the Way. Hence the Bodhisattva-bhumi says, 'One who with fixed determination vows bodhi alone is called bodhisattva.' Second, distinguished by the understanding-mind looking toward the principle: the ordinary beings cling to being and the two vehicles abide in non-being; they do not accord with the middle Way; therefore they are not called beings of the Way. Only the bodhisattva subtly lets go of being and non-being and accords with the middle Way; therefore he is called a being of the Way. Third, distinguished by the practice: in entering the Buddha-Dharma there are in general three: first the teaching, second the meaning, third the practice. The teaching is shallow, the meaning deep, and the practice is most supreme. The sravakas have dull faculties, named from the teaching; 'sravaka' (the hearer) is the teaching, hearing the voice and awakening to understanding, hence 'hearer' (sravaka). The pratyekabuddha is next superior, established by the meaning; 'pratyeka' (dependent) is the meaning, awakening to understanding on the conditions, hence 'dependent-awakened.' The bodhisattva is the most supreme, named from the practice: being able to accomplish the Way of benefiting self, benefiting others, and benefiting both; therefore he is called a being of the Way. Hence the Bodhisattva-bhumi says, 'The sravakas and pratyekabuddhas can save only themselves; the bodhisattva is not so, saving himself and saving others; therefore his Way is supreme.' Because the Way is supreme he is called a being of the Way. Gathering together is called 'together.'

Samantabhadra bodhisattva, Manjusri (Miaode) bodhisattva, Maitreya (Cishi) bodhisattva, and so forth, all the bodhisattvas of this Bhadra-kalpa (the Worthy Age). Moreover the sixteen worthies, headed by Bhadrapala: the bodhisattva Good Reflection, the bodhisattva Faith and Wisdom, the bodhisattva Emptiness and No-thing, the bodhisattva Supernatural Flower, the bodhisattva Light and Radiance, the bodhisattva Wisdom Supreme, the bodhisattva Wisdom Banner, the bodhisattva Serene Root, the bodhisattva Vow and Wisdom, the bodhisattva Fragrant Elephant, the bodhisattva Jewel Radiance, the bodhisattva Dwelling in the Middle, the bodhisattva Regulating Conduct, the bodhisattva Liberation. All these revere the virtue of the great being Samantabhadra.
[Commentary]

Next their names are listed. Within it, first those bodhisattvas who will become Buddhas in the Bhadra-kalpa are listed, and then, under 'Bhadrapala and the rest,' the bodhisattvas of the other kalpas are distinguished. Within the Bhadra-kalpa, Samantabhadra, Manjusri, and Maitreya are the three listed separately. Manjusri is Wenshu; Maitreya is Cishi, his surname being 'compassionate,' hence 'Compassionate Clan'; his name is Ajita, which here means 'No-Superior.' 'And so forth' are the other bodhisattvas of the Bhadra-kalpa; 'all the bodhisattvas of this Bhadra-kalpa' generally sums them by time. In clarifying the bodhisattvas of the other kalpas, sixteen worthies are briefly raised; 'the sixteen worthies headed by Bhadrapala' raises the beginning to include the rest, generally listing them; 'Good Reflection and the rest' lists individually those among their equals. 'All these revere the virtue of the great being Samantabhadra' reveals what they studied, and may also be called distinguishing the lower from the higher.

Next is the praise of their virtue, within which there are two divisions: first praising their twofold virtue of expedience and ultimate; second, from 'whose practice is pure' onward, praising their twofold virtue of self-benefit and benefiting others. Within the former there are three: first, from their own division briefly praising their virtue; second, from 'entering the Dharma-storehouse' onward, broadly praising their virtue in progressive advance; third, from 'perfect and complete virtue, wondrous' onward, jointly concluding the praise.
Possessing the immeasurable practices and vows of all bodhisattvas, abiding in all the dharmas of virtue, roaming the ten directions, employing the skillful means of expedience.
[Commentary]

In the first brief [praise], first the ultimate virtue is praised; from 'roaming' onward their expedient virtue is praised. In the ultimate, 'possessing the immeasurable practices and vows' means the practices are complete and full. 'Practice' means the six perfections and the four methods of gathering; 'vow' means the immeasurable bodhi practices and vows, as the Avatamsaka speaks. These they all possess. 'Abiding in all the dharmas of virtue' means the completed virtue is fully furnished; the virtue being accomplished it never retreats, hence 'abiding.' Having virtue it is accomplished, hence 'all.' 'Gong' (virtue) means function; all the practices benefit, hence 'merit' (gong); this merit is the virtue of good practice, hence 'virtue' (de). As the clear and cool and so forth are the virtue of water, hence 'virtue.' The sutra's spoken 'virtue and merit' has a common and a particular sense; in the common sense all practices are so, in the particular sense the practice of wisdom is called wisdom while the remaining precepts, giving, and so forth are called virtue; here the common is taken. The substance of virtue is called 'dharma.' In the expedient [praise], first 'roaming the ten directions' means the body is unobstructed; 'employing the skillful means of expedience' means the transforming activity is skillfully appropriate, appearing variously according to the fitness of beings; this is called 'expedient means.'
Above, their virtue was briefly praised according to their own division.

Below, their virtue is broadly praised according to the progressive advance. Within it, first their ultimate virtue is praised; from 'attaining Buddhahood in immeasurable worlds' onward, their expedient virtue is praised.
Entering the Dharma-storehouse of the Buddha, reaching in the ultimate the further shore.
[Commentary]

In the ultimate, first it says, 'entering the Dharma-storehouse of the Buddha'; to realize and attain is called 'entering.' 'The further shore reached in the ultimate' reveals the fruit as final; the further shore of nirvana, reached, is called 'ultimate.'
In immeasurable worlds manifesting the accomplishment of perfect enlightenment.
[Commentary]

In praising the expedient virtue, 'in immeasurable worlds manifesting the accomplishment of right enlightenment' praises it in general. This praises the progressive advance; therefore it raises the attainment of Buddhahood as the expedient virtue.

From 'dwelling in Tushita' below, it specifically reveals it. Within it, fully treated, there should be ten marks: first ascending to the Tushita heaven; second coming down and entering the womb; third abiding in the womb; fourth birth; fifth the mark of the child; sixth the mark of taking a consort; seventh the mark of leaving home; eighth the mark of accomplishing the Buddha-way; ninth the mark of turning the Dharma-wheel; tenth the mark of parinirvana. In the present text one is missing, the abiding in the womb, leaving nine marks.
Dwelling in the Tushita heaven, widely proclaiming the correct Dharma.
[Commentary]

In the first mark, 'dwelling in the Tushita heaven' is the body ascending to Tushita. Tushita was originally one name; the transmission makes the sound vary. This is translated 'splendid abundance,' also called 'contentment'; it is the fourth heaven of the desire-realm. Why is he born there? As the Nirvana explains, the Tushita heaven is supreme, and therefore he is born specifically there. In what is it supreme? The sutra itself explains: the upper heavens are dark and dull, the lower heavens are indulgent; this one has neither fault, hence it is called supreme. Moreover, cultivating giving and precepts one obtains the upper and lower heavens; cultivating giving, precepts, and concentration one is born in Tushita; therefore that heaven is supreme. One may ask, 'Tushita is the distracted ground of the desire-realm; how does cultivating concentration lead one to be born in that heaven?' The explanation is that this is not the concentration of the eight meditations, but rather, within the mind of thought-wisdom of the desire-realm, one cultivates the mindfulness of the Buddha samadhi and is born in that heaven, called 'born there in dependence on concentration,' as the Bodhisattva-bhumi [says]. There are many discriminations, which cannot be fully treated. 'Widely proclaiming the correct Dharma' is the transformation by speech. This completes the first mark.
Leaving that heavenly palace, descending his spirit into the mother's womb.
[Commentary]

This is the second mark. One may ask, 'Why does he leave the bliss of the highest heaven?' It is in order to cause the beings of the Jambudvipa to all receive the Buddha's grace and produce a mind of reverence and weight. Therefore he must leave it. How is this so? Because he leaves the heavenly bliss, the beings of Jambudvipa all think, 'The Buddha left heavenly bliss to be born in Jambudvipa out of compassion for us,' and produce a mind of reverence. One may ask, 'Of the four kinds of birth, why does the Tathagata especially accept womb-birth?' The explanation is that among the four births, egg-birth and moisture-birth have inferior retribution, so the Buddha is not born [in them]; though transformation-birth is supreme, it has many senses, so the Buddha is not born [in it]. As the Nirvana says, in brief there are eight senses. First, at the beginning of the kalpa beings were born by transformation, and at that time their afflictions had not yet arisen, so there was no need for the Buddha's transformation, and he did not appear. When the Buddha appears in the world beings are womb-born; to increase the power of co-born [beings], he accepts womb-birth. Second, to be born in a superior clan, showing forth the supremacy of the Dharma, he accepts womb-birth. Third, to be born in a royal line, to rely on it for protecting the Dharma, he accepts womb-birth. Fourth, wanting to teach people to respect the work of father and mother, he accepts womb-birth. Fifth, to be born in a superior clan in order to still people's pride, he accepts womb-birth. Sixth, to accept womb-birth in order to still people's slander — how is this so? If the Buddha were born by transformation, many would slander, saying the Buddha is an apparition and not real; to still this slander, therefore he is not born by transformation. Seventh, to leave a body for the benefit of later ages, he accepts womb-birth — how is this so? If the Buddha were born by transformation, he would again pass away by transformation, as the lightning is spent and nothing remains; the Buddha leaves a residual body and relics to benefit the future, therefore he accepts womb-birth. Eighth, to be the same as all the Buddhas, he accepts womb-birth; the Buddhas of the three times, transforming womb-born beings, by the Dharma accept womb-birth, therefore he must be the same as them. Possessing all these senses, he accepts womb-birth. This is the second, finished.
According to the other sutras and treatises, here one is missing the mark of abiding in the womb. Since this is what is lacking, the third mark is [hereby] concluded.

Born from the right side, taking seven steps as he walked, his light shining brilliantly, universally illuminating the ten directions, immeasurable buddha-lands quaking in six ways, he raised his voice and declared, 'I shall be in this world the supreme honored one.' Sakra and Brahma attended him, and gods and men turned to him in reverence.
[Commentary]

This is the fourth mark, birth. Within it there are three: first, the birth-place is extraordinary; second, from 'taking steps' onward, what is manifested is extraordinary; third, from 'Sakra and Brahma' onward, the gods and men revere and serve. In the first, being born from the mother's right side: the birth-place of worldly beings is impure, foul, and lowly, and the Buddha differs from them, therefore he is born from the right side. Though born from the right side, it is as emerging from clouds and mist; the mother's body is at ease, without effort and without pain. In the second, among the manifested wonders, first the extraordinary wonder of the body is made clear, and from 'raised his voice' onward the extraordinary wonder of speech. The body has three: first, in the ten directions he takes seven steps each, showing forth the heroic strength of a great man, and in the ten directions' realms stands forth alone without fear; second, the body-light universally illuminating causes people to be aware; third, from 'immeasurable' onward, the earth trembles, causing Mara to crouch in fear. The six kinds of quaking, as the Sutra of Stages [says], are: trembling, surging, shaking, quivering, roaring, and rising. Quaking is like a cart shaking; surging is like a spring welling up and also like a pot boiling; shaking is the downward [motion], as worldly empty things, when shaken, go down; quivering is the quaking motion that causes the mind to be aware, and even beings dwelling in the sky know it; roaring is the issuing of sound, the earth like a face rising. Above is the making clear of the body's extraordinary wonder; from 'raised his voice' onward is the extraordinary wonder of speech, self-proclaiming his honored title and causing people to come and take refuge. Above is the second, the manifested wonders. In the third section, the gods and men revere and serve; the text is clear and easy to know. The Buddha's virtue is deep and weighty, so he causes Sakra and Brahma to all come and attend him, and men and gods to turn to him in reverence. The fourth mark is finished.
